foods.name: Freshly cooked fish, served hot
foods.why: Hot off the grill and flaking apart, cooked fish is the default good choice. Fish is actively encouraged here: 1 to 3 serves a week, a serve being about 150g.

foods.name: Canned tuna, salmon and sardines
foods.why: Canning does all the safety work for you, and tinned fish is a brilliant omega-3 hit. A small tin of tuna counts as half a serve, so several tins a week is fine.

foods.name: Canned smoked oysters and mussels
foods.why: Smoked seafood is usually a no, but the tin changes the answer. Canning heat-treats the lot, so smoked oysters and mussels from a can are a green light.

foods.name: Freshly cooked prawns, lobster, crab and calamari
foods.why: Cooked fresh and served hot, the whole shellfish crew is yours. Heat is the entire trick, so tuck in while it is still steaming rather than saving it for later.

foods.name: Fish and chips
foods.why: Straight out of the fryer and piping hot, battered fish is a green light. One thing worth asking at the counter: if the fish is flake, that is shark, and shark has a mercury cap.

foods.name: Freshly made sushi with cooked fillings
foods.why: Rolled in front of you with cooked fillings and eaten straight away, sushi is a green light. Nothing raw, nothing smoked, and no time spent sitting in a fridge.

foods.name: Flake (shark), swordfish and marlin
foods.why: Heads up: flake at the fish and chip shop IS shark. Shark, swordfish, broadbill and marlin carry the most mercury, so it is one serve a fortnight and no other fish that fortnight.
foods.makeItGreen: Keep it to one 150g serve a fortnight and eat no other fish in that fortnight. Note the sources differ here: Monash IVF says once a week, the Royal Women's says once a fortnight, and we go with the stricter fortnight.
foods.swap: Ask the shop for snapper, whiting or flathead instead: same batter, same chips, no mercury cap.

foods.name: Orange roughy and catfish
foods.why: Orange roughy (sometimes sold as sea perch) and catfish sit mid-table for mercury. One serve a week, with no other fish that week, keeps you comfortably inside the limit.
foods.makeItGreen: One 150g serve a week, and make it the only fish that week.
foods.swap: Snapper, barramundi, whiting or tinned tuna, none of which come with a weekly cap.

foods.name: Sashimi, raw sushi and poke
foods.why: Raw fish can carry listeria, one of the few bugs that keeps growing in a cold fridge. Sashimi, raw nigiri and poke are benched for the next few months.
foods.makeItGreen: Rolls made fresh in front of you with cooked fillings, like teriyaki chicken, tinned tuna or avocado, are back on the menu.
foods.swap: A cooked-roll sushi night at home, or hot garlic prawns with rice.

foods.name: Pre-made or store-bought sushi
foods.why: Even with cooked fillings, sushi that has been sitting in a fridge or a display case has had time for listeria to settle in. It is the sitting, not the filling.
foods.makeItGreen: Sushi made fresh in front of you with cooked fillings, eaten straight away, is a green light.
foods.swap: A hot teriyaki chicken don, or home-made cooked rolls with tinned tuna and avo.

foods.name: Raw oysters
foods.why: Raw oysters filter everything the water has to offer and nothing gets cooked out. Shellfish this raw waits until after the birth.
foods.makeItGreen: Cooked hot right through, like oysters Kilpatrick bubbling out from under the grill, and they are back on.
foods.swap: Kilpatrick, oysters mornay, or a plate of hot salt and pepper squid.

foods.name: Ceviche
foods.why: Citrus firms the fish up so it looks cooked, but that is chemistry, not heat, and the bugs never got the memo. Ceviche still counts as raw.
foods.makeItGreen: Cook the fish right through and serve it hot with the same lime, chilli and coriander over the top.
foods.swap: Hot grilled fish tacos with lime, coriander and plenty of avo.

foods.name: Smoked salmon, smoked trout and gravlax
foods.why: Cold smoked fish is chilled, ready to eat and never actually cooked, which is exactly the setup listeria likes. Canned or cooked right through is a different story.
foods.makeItGreen: Cooked right through in a hot dish, like a salmon and leek pasta bake straight from the oven, and it is a green light.
foods.swap: Canned salmon with cream cheese on a toasted bagel does the same job.

foods.name: Pre-cooked cold prawns
foods.why: Sold ready-cooked and chilled, these may have been sitting around a while, and cold ready-to-eat seafood is listeria's favourite address. Heat is the fix.
foods.makeItGreen: Reheat them until they are steaming hot right through, or order them hot in the first place.
foods.swap: Hot garlic prawns, or a prawn stir-fry cooked until they curl and sizzle.

foods.name: Marinated mussels
foods.why: Marinated seafood from the deli fridge is ready to eat and has not been near heat since it was packed. Listeria is very comfortable in the cold.
foods.makeItGreen: Cook mussels fresh and eat them hot, straight out of the pot with the shells steaming.
foods.swap: A hot pot of steamed mussels in garlic and tomato, with bread for the sauce.
